As per the text normalization/standardization approach mentioned in Appendix Section C pp.21 in the paper Robust Speech Recognition via Large-Scale Weak Supervision. The BasicTextNormalizer does the following functionality:

Remove any phrases between matching brackets ([, ]).
Remove any phrases between matching parentheses ((, )).
Replace any markers, symbols, and punctuation characters with a space, i.e. when the Unicode category of each character in the NFKC-normalized string starts with M, S, or P.
make the text lowercase.
replace any successive whitespace characters with a space

def mismatches(make_case):
    """Run make_case(code, spec) -> (got_thunk, expected) for every language; return {code: got-or-exception} for failures."""
    bad = {}
    for code, spec in INDIC_TTS.items():
        got, expected = make_case(code, spec)
        try:
            value = got()
        except Exception as e:  # a crash is a failure to report, not to hide
            bad[code] = f"raised {type(e).__name__}: {e}"
            continue
        if value != expected:
            bad[code] = (value, expected)
    return bad


# Digits are spelled as words, and each number is replaced on its own: a "1" must not rewrite the "1" inside "10".
bad = mismatches(lambda code, spec: (lambda: spec["cls"]()("1 10"), f"{spoken(code, 1)} {spoken(code, 10)}"))
assert not bad, bad


# Default mode: a decimal number must not crash; each side of the dot is spelled and the dot is kept.
bad = mismatches(lambda code, spec: (lambda: spec["cls"]()("1.5"), f"{spoken(code, 1)}.{spoken(code, 5)}"))
assert not bad, bad


# tts_mode: a decimal is spoken as <whole> <point-word> <fraction>.
bad = mismatches(lambda code, spec: (lambda: spec["cls"](tts_mode=True)("1.5"), f"{spoken(code, 1)} {POINT[code]} {spoken(code, 5)}"))
assert not bad, bad

def fraction_expected(code):
    frac = f"{spoken(code, 2)} {spoken(code, 5)}" if code == "hi" else spoken(code, 25)
    return f"{spoken(code, 1)} {POINT[code]} {frac}"


bad = mismatches(lambda code, spec: (lambda: spec["cls"](tts_mode=True)("1.25"), fraction_expected(code)))

text:
A python package for text standardisation/normalization. It uses normalization algorithm mentioned in OpenAI whisper paper. Using Whisper normalization can cause issues in Indic languages and other low resource languages when using BasicTextNormalizer. So normalization in Indic languages is also implemented in this package which was derived from indic-nlp-library.
Humans behind
This package is a python implementation of the text standardisation/normalization approach which is being used in OpenAI whisper. The code was originally being released as open-source in Whisper source code. More details about the text normalization approach used by whisper can be found on Appendix Section C pp.21 the paper Robust Speech Recognition via Large-Scale Weak Supervision by OpenAI team.

title: whisper_normalizer
text:
Why should we normalize/standardize text?

In ASR systems it’s important to normalize the text to reduce unintentional penalties in metrics like WER, CER etc.
Text normalization/standardization is process of converting texts in different styles into a standardized form, which is a best-effort attempt to penalize only when a word error is caused by actually mistranscribing a word, and not by formatting or punctuation differences.(from Whisper paper)

title: whisper_normalizer

This package is a python implementation of the text standardisation/normalization approach which is being used in OpenAI whisper text normalizer. If you want to use just text normalization alone, it’s better to use this instead reimplementing the same thing. OpenAI approach of text normalization is very helpful and is being used as normalization step when evaluating competitive models like AssemblyAI Conformer-1 model.

from whisper_normalizer.english import EnglishTextNormalizer

normalizer = BasicTextNormalizer()

section: Using BasicTextNormalizer in your mother tongue might be a bad idea
text:
Using BasicTextNormalizer in your mother tongue might be a bad idea
Whisper Text Normalizer is not always recommended to be used. Dr Kavya Manohar has written a blogpost on why it might be a bad idea on her blopost titled Indian Languages and Text Normalization: Part 1.
If you need the basic normalizer for Indic or other scripts that use Unicode Mark characters, use BasicTextNormalizer(preserve_marks=True). This preserves combining marks such as Brahmic vowel signs and viramas while retaining the remaining basic normalization behavior.

This model extends Whisper_normalizer to support Indic languages as well.
The logic for normalization in Indic languages is derived from indic-nlp-library. The logic for Malayalam normalization is expanded beyond the Indic NLP library by MalayalamNormalizer.

title: whisper_normalizer
text:
TTS Mode for Indic Languages
tts_mode is not Indic-only: English, French, Spanish, Arabic, Russian and many other languages support it too (it needs pip install whisper_normalizer[tts]); see the capability table. This section describes the Indic behaviour.
Several Indic normalizers support a tts_mode=True option that converts text into a form suitable for text-to-speech synthesis. When enabled, the normalizer will:

Convert currency symbols to spoken forms (₹100 → “रुपये एक सौ”, $20 → “डॉलर बीस”)
Convert decimal numbers to spoken form (1.5 → “एक पॉइंट पांच”)
Expand URLs and domains to spoken form (https://example.com → “एच टी टी पी एस कोलन स्लैश स्लैश ई एक्स ए एम पी एल ई डॉट कॉम”)
Expand email addresses (user@example.com → “यूजर एट एक्साम्पल डॉट कॉम”)
Expand special symbols (& → ” or “, @ →” at “, % →” percent “, etc.)
Expand acronyms (NASA → “N A S A”)

Usage
from whisper_normalizer import Normalizer

# Pick a language; Normalizer.for_language("hi", tts_mode=True) is equivalent
normalizer = Normalizer("hi", tts_mode=True)
# Metadata: normalizer.language == "hi", .name == "Hindi", .tier == "dedicated"
result = normalizer("नमस्ते ₹100 और $20.50")
# Output: "नमस्ते रुपये एक सौ और डॉलर बीस पॉइंट पांच शून्य"
Or use the normalizer class directly:
from whisper_normalizer.indic import HindiNormalizer

normalizer = HindiNormalizer(tts_mode=True)
result = normalizer("Visit https://example.com or email user@example.com")
# Output: "visit एच टी टी पी एस कोलन स्लैश स्लैश ई एक्स ए एम पी एल ई डॉट कॉम or यूजर एट एक्साम्पल डॉट कॉम"


Option validation

As per the text normalization/standardization approach Appendix Section C pp.21 the paper Robust Speech Recognition via Large-Scale Weak Supervision. The EnglishTextNormalizer does the following functionality:

Remove any phrases between matching brackets ([, ]).
Remove any phrases between matching parentheses ((, )).
Remove any of the following words: hmm, mm, mhm, mmm, uh, um
Remove whitespace characters that comes before an apostrophe ’
Convert standard or informal contracted forms of English into the original form.
Remove commas (,) between digits
Remove periods (.) not followed by numbers
Remove symbols as well as diacritics from the text, where symbols are the characters with the Unicode category starting with M, S, or P, except period, percent, and currency symbols that may be detected in the next step.
Detect any numeric expressions of numbers and currencies and replace with a form using Arabic numbers, e.g. “Ten thousand dollars” → “$10000”.
Convert British spellings into American spellings.
Remove remaining symbols that are not part of any numeric expressions.
Replace any successive whitespace characters with a space.

tts_mode for English
With tts_mode=True the text is prepared for speech: written numbers stay words (the usual words-to-digits step is skipped), digits, currencies and percentages are spelled out, and a few symbols are spoken. Default behaviour is unchanged.

# tts_mode spells digits as words.
tts = EnglishTextNormalizer(tts_mode=True)
assert tts("I have 3 apples and 42 pears") == "i have three apples and forty two pears"


# Written numbers stay words in tts_mode: the usual words-to-digits step is skipped.
assert tts("I was born in nineteen eighty four") == "i was born in nineteen eighty four"
assert tts("a hundred apples") == "a hundred apples"

for text, expected in [

    ("£3", "three pounds"),
    ("only 5¢", "only five cents"),
]:

for text, expected in [
    ("50% off", "fifty percent off"),
    ("3.5% growth", "three point five percent growth"),
    ("pi is 3.14", "pi is three point one four"),
    ("exactly 3.50", "exactly three point five zero"),
    ("salt & pepper", "salt and pepper"),
    ("2 + 2 = 4", "two plus two equals four"),
    ("meet me @ noon", "meet me at noon"),
]:

Return the language registry in ISO-code order.

    language:str, **options

Normalize text for one language: Normalizer("hi", tts_mode=True)("...").
language accepts ISO codes ("hi"), BCP-47 tags ("hi-IN", "zh-Hans") and English names ("hindi"). Options such as tts_mode=True are validated against the selected language and raise ValueError if it does not accept them, instead of being ignored. Normalizer.for_language("hi") is an equivalent spelling.

LanguageSupport
def LanguageSupport(
    code:str, name:str, factory:Callable[..., Callable[[str], str]], capabilities:tuple[str, ...], tier:str,
    marks:Literal['kept', 'stripped']='kept'
)->None:
A supported language and the normalization level available for it.
tier is one of:

"dedicated": a normalizer written and reviewed for this language.
"script": no dedicated class yet, but the language shares a script with a dedicated normalizer that is reused as-is (for example Marathi reuses the Devanagari normalizer, without Hindi’s number/TTS tuning).
"generic": only conservative, script-safe cleanup is applied; no language-specific rules exist.

MultilingualTextNormalizer
def MultilingualTextNormalizer(
    lang:str='', tts_mode:bool=False
):
Conservative, script-safe normalization for languages without bespoke rules.



assert len(supported_languages()) == 101

tiers = {"dedicated": 0, "script": 0, "generic": 0}
for entry in supported_languages():
    tiers[entry.tier] += 1
assert tiers == {"dedicated": 15, "script": 4, "generic": 82}

# BCP-47 region/script subtags are accepted; only the primary language subtag
# drives selection.
assert Normalizer("french")("Vingt et un euros.") == "21 euros"
assert Normalizer("es-ES")("El total es 1.234,50.") == "el total es 1234.50"
assert Normalizer("Russian")("Privet, mir!") == "privet mir"
assert Normalizer("hi-IN")("नमस्ते, दुनिया!") == Normalizer("hi")("नमस्ते, दुनिया!")
assert Normalizer("en-IN")("Colour and favour.") == Normalizer("en")("Colour and favour.")

# ar/zh/ru must use their dedicated normalizers (from international.py), not
# the generic fallback: dedicated Chinese/Arabic normalization differs from
# the generic tier by converting written numerals and removing all
# inter-character whitespace, which the generic normalizer does not do.
assert Normalizer("zh")("你好，世界！") == "你好世界"
assert Normalizer("zh")("我有二十一個蘋果。") == "我有21個蘋果"
assert Normalizer("ar")("أَهْلًا، وَسَهْلًا!") == "اهلا وسهلا"

# Odia ("or") is a dedicated normalizer even though it isn't one of the ~99
# languages Whisper itself documents. "od-IN" and "odia" are accepted as
# aliases for the same "or" code.
assert LANGUAGE_REGISTRY["or"].tier == "dedicated"
assert Normalizer("od-IN")("2024") == Normalizer("or")("2024")
assert Normalizer("odia")("2024") == Normalizer("or")("2024")

# Script tier: Marathi (mr) and Assamese (as) now support tts_mode via
# indic_numtowords. Nepali (ne) and Sanskrit (sa) remain script-only (not
# covered by indic_numtowords).
assert LANGUAGE_REGISTRY["mr"].tier == "script"
assert isinstance(Normalizer("mr").normalizer, DevanagariNormalizer)
assert Normalizer("mr")("क: ख") == Normalizer("hi")("क: ख")  # shared Devanagari visarga rule
# Marathi now supports tts_mode via DevanagariNormalizer (indic_numtowords supports 'mr').
assert Normalizer("mr", tts_mode=True).tts_mode is True

assert LANGUAGE_REGISTRY["as"].tier == "script"
assert isinstance(Normalizer("as").normalizer, BengaliNormalizer)
assert Normalizer("as").normalizer.lang == "as"

# tts_mode is validated against the selected normalizer instead of being
# silently ignored or forwarded to a constructor that doesn't accept it.
assert Normalizer("hi", tts_mode=True).tts_mode is True
assert Normalizer("bn", tts_mode=True).tts_mode is True
# French now supports tts_mode via _LatinTextNormalizer (num2words converts digits to words).
assert Normalizer("fr", tts_mode=True).tts_mode is True

try:
    Normalizer("xx")
except ValueError as error:
    assert "Unsupported language" in str(error)
else:
    raise AssertionError("unknown languages must be rejected")

# Generic-tier smoke test: every generic-tier code must lowercase, strip
# punctuation and symbols (including emoji, which are Unicode Symbol
# category), collapse whitespace, and stay safe on empty/mixed-script input,
# without bespoke per-language fixtures.
generic_codes = [entry.code for entry in supported_languages() if entry.tier == "generic"]
assert len(generic_codes) == 82
for code in generic_codes:
    normalizer = Normalizer(code)
    assert normalizer("") == ""
    assert normalizer("HELLO, World!!") == "hello world"
    assert normalizer("Café 😀 مرحبا") == "café مرحبا"


# Per-language regression fixtures — dedicated and script tier

# Marathi (script tier): Devanagari normalisation + correct number words
mr = Normalizer('mr')
assert mr('क: ख') == Normalizer('hi')('क: ख')  # visarga rule shared
mr_tts = Normalizer('mr', tts_mode=True)
assert mr_tts.tts_mode is True
result_mr = mr_tts('मला 42 रुपये द्या')
assert '42' not in result_mr, f'MR TTS: digit not converted: {result_mr}'
# Marathi uses 'बेचाळीस', not Hindi 'बयालीस'
assert 'बेचाळीस' in result_mr, f'MR: wrong number word: {result_mr}'

# Assamese (script tier): Bengali normaliser + Assamese char remapping + TTS
as_norm = Normalizer('as')
assert as_norm.language == 'as'
as_tts = Normalizer('as', tts_mode=True)
result_as = as_tts('আমি 10 টকা')
assert '10' not in result_as, f'AS TTS: digit not converted: {result_as}'

# Nepali / Sanskrit: tts_mode unsupported
try:
    Normalizer('ne', tts_mode=True)
    raise AssertionError('ne should raise ValueError')
except ValueError as e:
    assert 'tts_mode' in str(e) or 'not supported' in str(e)

try:
    Normalizer('sa', tts_mode=True)
    raise AssertionError('sa should raise ValueError')
except ValueError as e:
    assert 'tts_mode' in str(e) or 'not supported' in str(e)

# Generic tier: smoke coverage for a representative sample
for code, sample, expected in [

The registry’s capability metadata is checked against real behaviour for every language, so the documented table cannot drift from what the normalizers do.

# tts_mode is advertised exactly when it can be constructed, and then it spells digits as words.
bad = {}
for entry in supported_languages():
    try:
        n = Normalizer(entry.code, tts_mode=True)
    except ValueError:
        constructible = False
    else:
        constructible = True
        spoken = n("5")
        if any(ch.isdigit() for ch in spoken):
            bad[entry.code] = f"tts_mode left a digit in {spoken!r}"
    if constructible != ("tts_mode" in entry.capabilities):
        bad[entry.code] = f"advertises tts_mode={'tts_mode' in entry.capabilities} but constructible={constructible}"
assert not bad, bad


# digits_to_words says when digits become words, and matches what default mode really does for all languages:
# "always" (Indic family), "tts_mode" (only with tts_mode=True) or "never" (tts_mode unavailable).
bad = {}
for entry in supported_languages():
    spelled_by_default = not any(ch.isdigit() for ch in Normalizer(entry.code)("5"))
    if (entry.digits_to_words == "always") != spelled_by_default:
        bad[entry.code] = (entry.digits_to_words, "spelled by default" if spelled_by_default else "digits kept")
    # Outside the Indic family, "never" is exactly "tts_mode unavailable".
    if entry.digits_to_words != "always" and (entry.digits_to_words == "never") != ("tts_mode" not in entry.capabilities):
        bad[entry.code] = (entry.digits_to_words, entry.capabilities)
assert not bad, bad
assert {e.code for e in supported_languages() if e.digits_to_words == "always"} == {
    "as", "bn", "gu", "hi", "kn", "ml", "mr", "ne", "or", "pa", "sa", "ta", "te"}
assert Normalizer("en").tts_mode is False and [e for e in supported_languages() if e.code == "en"][0].digits_to_words == "tts_mode"


# marks says whether combining marks survive normalization ("kept") or are removed ("stripped"); it is checked against
# real behaviour for every dedicated and script-tier language, plus the generic tier.
import unicodedata


def count_marks(s):
    return sum(unicodedata.category(ch).startswith("M") for ch in unicodedata.normalize("NFD", s))


INDIC_BASE = {"hi": 0x0900, "mr": 0x0900, "ne": 0x0900, "sa": 0x0900, "bn": 0x0980, "as": 0x0980, "pa": 0x0A00,
              "gu": 0x0A80, "or": 0x0B00, "ta": 0x0B80, "te": 0x0C00, "kn": 0x0C80, "ml": 0x0D00}
MARK_SAMPLES = {code: chr(b + 0x15) + chr(b + 0x3F) for code, b in INDIC_BASE.items()}  # KA + vowel sign I
MARK_SAMPLES.update({"en": "café", "fr": "café", "es": "niño", "ar": "أَهْلًا", "ru": "йод", "de": "café", "th": "ที่"})
NO_MARKS_IN_SCRIPT = {"zh"}  # Chinese has no combining marks to keep or strip

bad = {}
checked_marks = set()
for entry in supported_languages():
    # Every generic-tier language runs the same script-safe cleanup, so one accented sample covers each of them.
    sample = MARK_SAMPLES.get(entry.code) or ("café" if entry.tier == "generic" else None)
    if sample is None:
        assert entry.code in NO_MARKS_IN_SCRIPT, f"no marks sample for {entry.code}"
        continue
    checked_marks.add(entry.code)
    out = Normalizer(entry.code)(sample)
    expected_marks = 0 if entry.marks == "stripped" else count_marks(sample)
    if count_marks(out) != expected_marks:
        bad[entry.code] = (entry.marks, sample, out)
assert not bad, bad
assert {e.code for e in supported_languages() if e.marks == "stripped"} == {"ar", "en"}
# Every language except Chinese (no combining marks) is checked: 100 of 101.
assert len(checked_marks) == 100 and checked_marks == {e.code for e in supported_languages()} - NO_MARKS_IN_SCRIPT

The table in README.md and nbs/index.ipynb is generated from the registry by capability_section() below; the test pins both files to it, so it cannot go stale.

import json
from pathlib import Path

from indic_numtowords import supported_langs as _numtowords_langs


def capability_section():
    """Markdown for the supported-languages table: one row per dedicated/script language, plus a generic-tier summary."""
    rows = ["| Language | Code | Normalizer | Tier | Digits → words | Marks | `tts_mode` |", "|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|"]
    entries = sorted((e for e in supported_languages() if e.tier != "generic"), key=lambda e: (e.tier != "dedicated", e.name))
    for e in entries:
        cls = getattr(e.factory, "func", e.factory).__name__
        digits = e.digits_to_words
        if digits == "always" and e.code not in _numtowords_langs:
            digits += " (Hindi number words)"
        tts = "yes" if "tts_mode" in e.capabilities else "no"
        rows.append(f"| {e.name} | `{e.code}` | `{cls}` | {e.tier} | {digits} | {e.marks} | {tts} |")
    generic = [e for e in supported_languages() if e.tier == "generic"]
    with_tts = sum("tts_mode" in e.capabilities for e in generic)
    summary = (
        f"The other {len(generic)} languages use the generic tier: Unicode NFC, brackets and punctuation removed, "
        f"case folded, combining marks kept. Digits become words only with `tts_mode=True`, which {with_tts} of them support."
    )
    return "\n".join(rows) + "\n\n" + summary

def llm_wer(

)->float:
Return Sarvam-style LLM-WER using an application-supplied conservative judge.
The judge receives each non-exact aligned span and must return True only when it is certainly semantically and phonetically equivalent. The final numerator is capped at the reference length, preventing repeated hallucinations from dominating aggregate results.

Return Orthographically-Informed WER as a fraction.
reference fixes the denominator to the original transcript, as in an OI benchmark. When omitted, the first alternative in every segment is treated as that original transcript.
